Perhaps you are intending to ask, "Do we really need a dedicated swap partition?"

One problem with a dedicated partition is that it consumes disk space, even when you are not using it. It is always at maximum size.

Recently, in Ubuntu based systems for example, a swap partition is no longer used. Instead, a swap file is created. This can grow or shrink in size, as necessary. That is an improvement, I think. I would like to know why a swap file instead of a partition wasn't used before.

Before people used to have spinning, magnetic, hard disk drives. (Some of us still do. *yells at children to get off his lawn*) A swap file, that was not pre-allocated, might get smeared all over the disk. One that "grow[s] or shrink[s] in size" might also get spread around. It took a long time for the disks to seek should the OS need to read or write to far distant sectors. I think this is probably why swap is/was a dedicated partition. All the sectors used for swap are close to each other.
